clinicalPearls: Gastroparesis is delayed gastric emptying in the absence of mechanical obstruction, presenting with nausea, vomiting, early satiety, bloating, and postprandial fullness
The commonest identifiable causes are diabetes mellitus and prior gastric or vagal surgery, but many cases are idiopathic and some follow a viral illness
Mechanical obstruction must be excluded, typically by endoscopy, before the diagnosis is made
A scintigraphic gastric emptying study of a solid meal is the standard confirmatory test, with wireless motility capsule and breath tests as alternatives
Medications that slow gastric emptying, especially opioids and GLP-1 receptor agonists, can cause or worsen symptoms and should be reviewed
Management combines dietary modification toward small, low-fat, low-fibre meals with prokinetic and antiemetic therapy
Refractory disease may require enteral feeding beyond the stomach, gastric electrical stimulation, or endoscopic pyloric procedures
reference.pathophysiology: Gastroparesis arises from impaired neuromuscular coordination of gastric emptying. Injury to the vagus nerve, abnormalities of the interstitial cells of Cajal that pace gastric contractions, smooth muscle dysfunction, and autonomic neuropathy disrupt fundic accommodation, antral contractility, and pyloric relaxation. In diabetes, chronic hyperglycaemia and autonomic neuropathy impair motility, and acute hyperglycaemia itself further slows emptying. The result is retained gastric contents, which produce nausea, vomiting, and impaired nutrient and drug absorption.
additionalDifferentials: Cyclic vomiting syndrome or cannabinoid hyperemesis
additionalInvestigations: Upper endoscopy to exclude mechanical obstruction
Wireless motility capsule or breath test as alternatives
Blood glucose and HbA1c assessment in diabetic patients
Review of medications affecting gastric motility
Nutritional and electrolyte assessment in severe or chronic disease
redFlags: Intractable vomiting with dehydration and electrolyte disturbance
Features suggesting mechanical obstruction or malignancy
Marked or unstable glycaemic control complicating diabetic gastroparesis
reference.prognosis: Gastroparesis is often a chronic, fluctuating condition; many patients achieve reasonable symptom control with diet and medication, but a subset have refractory, disabling symptoms with recurrent hospitalisation and nutritional compromise.
pitfalls: Diagnosing gastroparesis without first excluding mechanical obstruction
Overlooking opioids or GLP-1 receptor agonists as reversible contributors
Ignoring hyperglycaemia, which acutely delays emptying and undermines treatment
Missing alternative diagnoses such as rumination or cyclic vomiting that mimic gastroparesis
